why: Colonoscopy works and is widely avoided, so the market was people skipping screening entirely rather than choosing between tests. He ran a 10,000-patient trial to win FDA approval and, critically, a simultaneous Medicare national coverage decision, so the test was reimbursed from launch.
obst: Exact Sciences had almost no cash and no product when he arrived in 2009; the US Preventive Services Task Force gave Cologuard only lukewarm language in 2016, briefly halving the stock, and Guardant's blood test threatened to make a stool test obsolete.
turn: The August 2014 FDA approval of Cologuard alongside a parallel Medicare coverage decision, the first joint review of its kind, which gave the test a paying market on day one.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 24 Jul 2026: 649,747 Progressive shares held directly, in the 401(k), by her husband and his trust; PGR closed $219.28 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial share count x closing price; excludes unvested restricted equity
did: Joined Progressive in 1988 as a claims adjuster, ran claims and then the personal lines business, and became chief executive in 2016, the first woman to run a major US auto insurer. Progressive passed Allstate to become the second-largest US auto insurer under her.
why: Auto insurance is won on segmentation: whoever prices risk most granularly keeps the profitable drivers and sheds the rest. She backed telematics through Snapshot and bought a home product so Progressive could hold bundling households, then raised rates faster than rivals when 2022 claims inflation hit.
obst: She inherited a book leaking customers to insurers that could bundle home coverage, and in 2022 used-car and repair inflation drove Progressive's combined ratio above 100, forcing her to halt advertising and shed policies for more than a year before growth resumed.
turn: The 2015 purchase of a controlling stake in ARX Holding, owner of American Strategic Insurance, which gave Progressive a home product and let it compete for bundled households.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 7 Aug 2026: 1,086,869 RPM International shares held directly, via the Thomas C. Sullivan Irrevocable Trust and the 401(k); RPM closed $108.63 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial share count x closing price; excludes stock appreciation rights
did: Third-generation chief executive of RPM International in Medina, Ohio, the specialty coatings group behind Rust-Oleum, DAP, Zinsser and Tremco. He joined in 1987, became CEO in 2002 and took revenue past 7 billion dollars through more than 100 acquisitions.
why: RPM buys small niche coatings and sealant firms and leaves their brands, managers and sales forces alone, supplying only purchasing scale and capital. Coatings are a low share of a project's cost but high consequence, so specification stickiness protects price and founders sell for less than to an integrator.
obst: Asbestos liability from the Bondex subsidiary nearly sank the company; he put it into Chapter 11 in 2010 and spent four years negotiating before a 797 million dollar trust settlement in 2014. Elliott Management then ran an activist campaign in 2018 forcing margin targets and board changes.
turn: The 2014 Bondex asbestos trust settlement, which capped a liability that had frozen the stock for a decade and let him resume buying companies.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 25 Jun 2026: 950,839 Sun Communities shares held directly, by spouse and an irrevocable trust; SUI closed $121.66 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed common share count x closing price; excludes operating partnership units not reported on the Form 4
did: Built Sun Communities from his family's Michigan manufactured-housing parks into the largest US owner of manufactured-home and RV communities, taking it public in 1993 and buying Safe Harbor Marinas for 2.1 billion dollars in 2020. He stepped back from the CEO role in 2025.
why: A manufactured-home community is effectively a land lease: the resident owns a house that cannot be moved economically, so turnover is low, rents rise steadily and capital spending stays small. Local zoning has blocked nearly all new communities for decades, so supply is fixed and he could roll up the class.
obst: The company carried heavy leverage into the 2008 crash, when manufactured-home lending vanished and occupancy fell; Land and Buildings then ran an activist campaign in 2024 attacking the marina purchase and the UK holiday-park business, and he left the CEO job in 2025.
turn: The 2020 purchase of Safe Harbor Marinas, which applied the same fixed-supply land-lease logic to boat slips and opened a second asset class.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 4 Aug 2026: 554,528 Generac Holdings shares held directly; GNRC closed $205.98 on 21 Aug 2026

did: Joined Generac in Waukesha as an accountant in 1994, became chief financial officer and then chief executive in 2008, took the generator maker public in 2010 and built it into the dominant US home standby brand with roughly three quarters of the market.
why: A home standby generator is bought in the week after an outage, so the winner is whoever already has installed dealer capacity in the affected region. He spent years signing and training independent electrical contractors, so when a storm hit, only Generac had installers who could quote same day.
obst: He took over in 2008 with the company owned by CCMP Capital and loaded with buyout debt in the middle of the financial crisis; a 2022 recall of about 64,000 portable generators over finger amputation risk and a short-seller report on its SnapRS solar component then battered the stock.
turn: The 2010 IPO and the shift from selling a machine to selling outage protection through a trained dealer network, which turned every weather event into demand the company could actually fill.
